_doc: SELECT ALL SELECTS TOP-LEVEL OBJECTS, AND SELECTION ORDER IS PART OF THE
DOCUMENT — the cross-language family for transcripts/LAYER_STRUCTURE.md
§16 (D2, RULED 2026-07-28: 'keep the Rust shape') and §10 (D6, RULED
2026-07-28: JasSwift's Selection becomes an ordered array).
WHY THIS FAMILY COULD NOT EXIST BEFORE TODAY, twice over:
* op_apply had NO select_all verb in either port, so nothing shared
could reach Select All at all. That is how JasSwift's group-expanding
version survived unadjudicated (§16.1).
* the canonical-JSON selection serializer SORTED by path in both ports,
so no golden anywhere could see selection ORDER. That is how D6 —
measured as ten different orders over ten processes — stayed green.
The sort is gone; these goldens pin emission order.
THE DOCUMENT (select_all_top_level.svg; SVG px -> document pt is x3/4,
so x=32 lands at 24):
[0]     Layer 'Alpha'
[0,0]      rect  'solo-a'
[0,1]      group 'Trio'    -- THREE children
[1]     Layer 'Beta'
[1,0]      group 'Pair'    -- two children
[1,1]      rect  'solo-b'
So Select All must yield FOUR entries — [0,0] [0,1] [1,0] [1,1] — one per
top-level object, a group counting as ONE. Before the ruling JasSwift
yielded NINE: it delegated to selectFlat, whose group branch inserts the
group AND every unlocked grandchild. §16.2 is why that is a defect rather
than a competing design: no operation has a coherent reading of a set
containing an element and its own descendants — translate it and the group
moves by 24 while each child, already carried by its parent, moves again.
SELECTION-ONLY: select_all and add_to_selection are non-undoable, so these
cases journal nothing and the checkpoint_equivalence gate replays an empty
prefix. Both verbs route through the PRODUCTION Controller mutator; a verb
that re-implemented the walk would be a decoy that never goes red.
name: select_all_family_setup_is_two_layers_a_trio_and_a_pair

_doc: THE HEADLINE. Four entries, one per top-level object, in document order. A group counts as ONE (§16.3). Nine entries here is the pre-ruling JasSwift shape.
name: select_all_selects_top_level_objects_a_group_counting_as_one

_doc:
§16.4 (RULED 2026-07-29). The MARQUEE asks 'did anything inside the band match?' about a group's members, but ANSWERS with the group alone -- the same shape Select All produces (§16.3). This case therefore shares select_all_top_level_expected.json with the Select All case above: the two operations must land on the SAME selection for this document, and a shared golden makes that agreement structural rather than coincidental. If either drifts, this reds.
BEFORE THE RULING this branch pushed the group AND every unlocked member, nine entries where Select All gave four, and the file was named 'marquee_expands'. That shape is the one no operation reads coherently: copy_selection copies the group whole and then copies each member INTO the source group, so marquee-then-duplicate left the SOURCE holding four children instead of two. Move and delete survived it only by accident -- delete sorts paths descending, and move writes absolute positions read from the pristine document.
name: a_marquee_and_select_all_agree_on_the_same_top_level_objects

_doc: Select All is ancestor-aware about lock (§13): the locked layer contributes nothing, a locked element and a locked group are skipped, and 'Mixed Group' comes in as ONE entry even though one of its members is locked — because Select All never looks inside a group at all.
name: select_all_skips_locked_by_inheritance_and_still_counts_a_group_as_one

_doc: D6 ORDER, on the SHIFT-MARQUEE. Marquee everything (FOUR top-level entries since §16.4), then shift-marquee the solo rect at [0,0] alone: the XOR drops it and the other THREE must come back in their original order. Both ports build that result by walking the document, so a Set would lose the ordering this pins.
name: extend_marquee_deselects_one_and_keeps_the_others_in_order

_doc: D6 ORDER, on a COPY — and, since 2026-07-28, §19 (RULED by JYH: 'yes document order'). copy_selection walks the selection in DESCENDING path order so its insertions do not shift earlier paths, and THAT STAYS, load-bearing; what changed is that the selection it leaves behind is now sorted into DOCUMENT order instead of coming out in the walk's order as a byproduct. Two contiguous rects duplicated at dx=dy=6 give elements [a a' b b'] and selection [[0,1],[0,3]] — the two copies, back-to-front. This golden used to read [[0,2],[0,1]], and that was not merely reversed: [0,2] named b, THE SOURCE, because the later insertion at [0,0] shifted b up one slot after the walk had already recorded its copy path. The artist-visible consequence is one step away — a Copy after the duplicate emits this order onto the clipboard — and is gated in-port in both ports (Rust a_duplicate_then_copy_emits_the_copies_in_document_order, Swift DuplicateCopyOrderTests), because neither port has a copy-to-clipboard op verb for the corpus to drive.
name: copy_of_a_two_element_selection_emits_a_deterministic_order

_doc: §19, THE DISCRIMINATING CASE. Two elements can only be in one of two orders, so the contiguous case above cannot tell a SORT from a REVERSAL, and on its own it reads like an order bug and nothing more. Here the duplicated pair is NON-CONTIGUOUS — green at [0,1] and yellow at [0,3] of four rects — which is the shape §19 itself names. The descending walk copies yellow first, recording [0,4], then copies green; that second insertion shifts everything above it by one, so the recorded [0,4] silently stops naming yellow's COPY and starts naming yellow, THE SOURCE. The document that comes out is red@0 green@30 green'@36 blue@60 yellow@90 yellow'@96, and the ruled selection is [[0,2],[0,5]] — the two copies, in document order. The shipped answer was [[0,4],[0,2]]: reverse order AND a source. A fix that only sorts gives [[0,2],[0,4]], ascending and still wrong, and this case is what separates the two. Distinct fills make the identity legible in the golden rather than inferable from indices.
name: duplicating_a_noncontiguous_pair_selects_both_copies_not_a_source

_doc: §19, ACROSS PARENTS AND ACROSS DEPTHS — the case that makes the path-rewrite RULE watchable rather than just its outcome on one flat layer. Duplicate three things at once in this family's own setup: solo-a at [0,0], t3 at [0,1,2] (the last child of the Trio group), and solo-b at [1,1] (in the OTHER layer). The descending walk copies solo-b, then t3, then solo-a — and that last insertion, at [0,1], is the interesting one: it pushes the Trio group from [0,1] to [0,2], so the copy path already recorded for t3' has to travel from [0,1,3] to [0,2,3], while the copy path recorded for solo-b' must NOT move at all, because it lives under a different parent. Ruled answer [[0,1],[0,2,3],[1,2]] — three copies, document order. FOUR SEPARATE MUTATIONS RED THIS ONE CASE, which is why it is worth its bytes: dropping the sort gives [[1,2],[0,2,3],[0,1]]; dropping the rewrite entirely gives [0,1,3], a path into a rect; rewriting without checking the parent prefix drags solo-b' to [1,3], a slot that does not exist; and weakening the index test from >= to > leaves t3' at [0,1,3] — the boundary case is real precisely because an insertion AT a container's own index moves that whole container and everything under it.
name: duplicating_across_parents_and_depths_rewrites_only_the_paths_that_moved

_doc: D6 DEDUP. Selection is an ordered array in both ports now, so nothing deduplicates for free: add_to_selection must refuse a path it already holds. This case would go RED with a SECOND {kind:all, path:[0,1]} entry if the guard were dropped from either port — which is exactly the mutation that proves it.
name: add_to_selection_twice_on_one_path_yields_one_entry

_doc: D6 ORDER, on the additive seam. add_to_selection APPENDS: the entries come out in the order they were added, [1,1] then [0,0], not sorted into document order. A Set could not express this at all.
name: add_to_selection_appends_in_the_order_the_paths_were_added
